definition: The four guarantees of a classic database transaction: atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability.
A contrasting design philosophy for distributed stores: basically available, soft state and eventually consistent, favoring availability over strict consistency.
A group of operations the database treats as one unit: either all of its changes are applied or none are.
A setting (read committed, repeatable read, snapshot, serializable) that controls which anomalies concurrent transactions may observe.
Reading data written by another transaction that has not committed yet and may still be rolled back.
Reading the same row twice in one transaction and getting different values because another transaction committed a change in between.
Re-running a range query inside one transaction and seeing new or missing rows because another transaction inserted or deleted matching rows.
An anomaly where two transactions read the same value and both write back a result based on it, so one update silently overwrites the other.
An anomaly where two transactions read overlapping data, each writes a different row, and together they violate an invariant that neither broke alone.
The strongest isolation guarantee: the outcome of concurrent transactions equals some serial, one-at-a-time execution order.
Each transaction reads from a consistent snapshot taken at its start, preventing most anomalies but still allowing write skew.
Multi-version concurrency control: the database keeps several versions of a row so readers see a consistent snapshot without blocking writers.
A log to which every change is appended and flushed before it is applied to the data files, enabling crash recovery and replication.
An auxiliary data structure that lets the database find rows by a key without scanning the whole table, at the cost of extra storage and slower writes.
A balanced, wide, sorted tree structure used by most relational indexes, giving logarithmic lookups and efficient range scans.
A log-structured merge tree: writes go to memory and sequential sorted files that are merged in the background, favoring write-heavy workloads.
An index on several columns in a fixed order; it helps queries that filter on a leftmost prefix of those columns.
An index that contains every column a query needs, so the query is answered from the index alone without touching the table.
An index on a column other than the primary key, allowing lookups by other attributes; in sharded stores it may be local or global.
The strategy the optimizer chooses to run a query, showing which indexes, join order and scan types it will use; inspected with EXPLAIN.
Reading every row of a table to answer a query, typically because no usable index exists; cost grows linearly with table size.
A column or set of columns that uniquely identifies each row in a table and is usually backed by an index.
A column that references the primary key of another table, letting the database enforce that related rows exist.
Organizing a schema so each fact is stored once, removing redundancy and update anomalies at the price of more joins.
Deliberately duplicating data to make reads cheaper, accepting extra storage and the burden of keeping copies consistent.
A relational database that stores data in tables with a fixed schema, queries it with SQL and typically offers ACID transactions and joins.
A family of non-relational stores (key-value, document, wide-column, graph) that trade joins and rigid schemas for flexibility and horizontal scale.
A database that maps unique keys to opaque values and supports very fast get, put and delete by key, such as Redis or DynamoDB.
A database that stores self-contained, semi-structured documents (usually JSON) and can index and query their fields, such as MongoDB.
A database that organizes data into rows with flexible column families, optimized for huge write volumes and key-based access, such as Cassandra.
A database that stores nodes and edges as first-class citizens and answers relationship-heavy queries by traversal, such as Neo4j.
Online transaction processing: workloads of many small, concurrent reads and writes on current data, such as order entry.
Online analytical processing: workloads of large scans and aggregations over historical data, usually on columnar storage.
Storing each column's values together rather than each row's, which compresses well and speeds up analytic queries that read few columns.
Keeping copies of the same data on multiple nodes for fault tolerance, read scaling and lower latency to distant users.
A scheme where one node accepts all writes and streams changes to followers that serve reads; also called primary-replica or master-slave.
A scheme where several nodes accept writes and replicate them to each other, which helps multi-region writes but requires conflict resolution.
A scheme where any replica accepts writes and clients read and write to several replicas, relying on quorums and repair (Dynamo style).
The delay before a write on the leader becomes visible on a follower, causing stale reads from replicas.
A follower copy used to serve read queries, scaling read throughput while writes still go to the leader.
Splitting a dataset across multiple nodes so each holds only a portion, scaling both storage and write throughput.
The attribute whose value decides which shard stores a record; a poor choice causes skew and hot partitions.
A shard that receives disproportionate traffic, becoming a bottleneck while other shards sit idle.
A way to map keys to nodes on a hash ring so that adding or removing a node moves only a small fraction of keys.
One of many points a physical node occupies on a consistent-hash ring, used to even out load and speed up rebalancing.
Changing how data is split across shards, such as adding shards, which requires moving data while the system keeps serving traffic.
A system that stores structured, cleaned historical data in a columnar layout for analytics and reporting.
A large repository of raw data in many formats, usually on object storage, kept cheaply and structured only when read.
